title: Value functions: LAG, LEAD, FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTH_VALUE
summary_md: Read a value from another row of the window: previous or next row, first or last row of the group, or the nth row, plus the frame trap that breaks LAST_VALUE.

sections.heading: LAG and LEAD: look at a neighbouring row
sections.body_md:
- `LAG` reads a value from an earlier row, `LEAD` from a later row, in the window's `ORDER BY`. No self-join needed.
- The first row has no previous row, so `LAG` returns NULL there (and `LEAD` on the last row) unless you supply a `default`.
- `PARTITION BY` restarts the neighbour lookup per group: the first row of each group gets NULL/default, never a value from the previous group.
- `ORDER BY` inside `OVER` is required. Add a tiebreaker if two rows can share the sort key.
- `WHERE` runs before window functions. Filtering rows out first removes them as neighbours; filter after (CTE/subquery) if the boundary row must stay visible.

syntax.mysql:
LAG(expr [, offset [, default]])  OVER ([PARTITION BY p] ORDER BY o)
LEAD(expr [, offset [, default]]) OVER ([PARTITION BY p] ORDER BY o)
syntax.tsql:
LAG(expr [, offset [, default]])  OVER ([PARTITION BY p] ORDER BY o)
LEAD(expr [, offset [, default]]) OVER ([PARTITION BY p] ORDER BY o)

args.name: expr
args.meaning: The column or expression to read from the neighbouring row.

args.name: offset
args.meaning: How many rows back (LAG) or forward (LEAD). Optional, default 1. Must be a non-negative integer constant.

args.name: default
args.meaning: Value returned when the neighbour row does not exist. Optional, default NULL. Not applied when the neighbour exists but its value is NULL.

args.name: PARTITION BY p
args.meaning: Optional. Neighbours are only looked up inside the same group.

args.name: ORDER BY o
args.meaning: Defines 'previous' and 'next'. Add an id to break ties.

examples.title: Previous and next month revenue
examples.explain_md: Each row shows its neighbours. Jan 2023 is the first month overall, so its previous revenue is NULL.
examples.mysql:
SELECT month_start, revenue,
       LAG(revenue)  OVER (ORDER BY month_start) AS prev_revenue,
       LEAD(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month_start) AS next_revenue
FROM monthly_revenue
ORDER BY month_start
LIMIT 5;
examples.tsql:
SELECT TOP (5) month_start, revenue,
       LAG(revenue)  OVER (ORDER BY month_start) AS prev_revenue,
       LEAD(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month_start) AS next_revenue
FROM monthly_revenue
ORDER BY month_start;

examples.title: Default value and offset 2
examples.explain_md: `LAG(revenue, 1, 0)` replaces the missing first neighbour with 0. `LAG(revenue, 2)` looks two rows back, so both Jan and Feb are NULL. A default only fills 'no row', not a stored NULL.
examples.mysql:
SELECT month_start, revenue,
       LAG(revenue, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY month_start) AS prev_or_zero,
       LAG(revenue, 2)    OVER (ORDER BY month_start) AS two_months_ago
FROM monthly_revenue
ORDER BY month_start
LIMIT 4;
examples.tsql:
SELECT TOP (4) month_start, revenue,
       LAG(revenue, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY month_start) AS prev_or_zero,
       LAG(revenue, 2)    OVER (ORDER BY month_start) AS two_months_ago
FROM monthly_revenue
ORDER BY month_start;

examples.title: Next event per user (LEAD with PARTITION BY)
examples.explain_md: The last event of each user has no next row, so the default 'END' appears. User boundaries are respected: user 1's last row does not borrow user 2's first event.
examples.mysql:
SELECT user_id, event_id, event_type,
       LEAD(event_type, 1, 'END') OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_id) AS next_event
FROM events
ORDER BY user_id, event_ts, event_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT user_id, event_id, event_type,
       LEAD(event_type, 1, 'END') OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_id) AS next_event
FROM events
ORDER BY user_id, event_ts, event_id;

examples.title: Trap: WHERE removes the neighbour
examples.explain_md: Filtering to 2024 *before* the window means Jan 2024 cannot see Dec 2023, so its `prev_revenue` is NULL even though the data exists. Compute LAG over all rows first, then filter (see the period-comparisons page).
examples.mysql:
SELECT month_start, revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month_start) AS prev_revenue
FROM monthly_revenue
WHERE month_start >= '2024-01-01'
ORDER BY month_start
LIMIT 3;
examples.tsql:
SELECT TOP (3) month_start, revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month_start) AS prev_revenue
FROM monthly_revenue
WHERE month_start >= '2024-01-01'
ORDER BY month_start;

pitfalls_md: `LAG(x, 0)` is legal and returns the current row; offsets must not be negative or a column.
The default argument must be type-compatible with `expr`.
A LAG over rows with gaps in time (missing months) still returns the previous *existing* row, not the previous calendar period.

sections.heading: Differences from the previous row and time gaps
sections.body_md:
- Change since last row: `value - LAG(value) OVER (...)`. The first row is NULL because `LAG` is NULL.
- Time since last row: compute the previous timestamp with `LAG`, then diff it in the outer expression.
- MySQL: `DATEDIFF(date1, date2)` is days, `date1 - date2` order. `TIMESTAMPDIFF(unit, earlier, later)` for other units.
- SQL Server: `DATEDIFF(unit, earlier, later)` always takes the unit first and the earlier date first.
- Filter on a status *before* LAG when only some rows should count (for example only completed orders); the neighbour is then the previous *matching* row.

syntax.mysql:
-- MySQL
DATEDIFF(later_date, earlier_date)               -- days
TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE, earlier_ts, later_ts)
syntax.tsql:
-- SQL Server
DATEDIFF(DAY, earlier_date, later_date)
DATEDIFF(MINUTE, earlier_ts, later_ts)

args.name: DATEDIFF (MySQL)
args.meaning: DATEDIFF(a, b) = a - b in days. Later date goes first.

args.name: DATEDIFF (SQL Server)
args.meaning: DATEDIFF(unit, start, end) = end - start. Unit first, earlier date first.

args.name: TIMESTAMPDIFF(unit, start, end)
args.meaning: MySQL: whole units from start to end. unit is MINUTE, HOUR, DAY...

examples.title: Revenue change versus the previous month
examples.explain_md: Subtracting `LAG` gives the absolute change. Jan 2023 is NULL (no previous month). The CTE keeps all months so the window sees them, then the outer query trims.
examples.mysql:
WITH m AS (
  SELECT month_start, revenue,
         revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month_start) AS change_vs_prev
  FROM monthly_revenue
)
SELECT month_start, revenue, change_vs_prev
FROM m
WHERE month_start <= '2023-06-01'
ORDER BY month_start;
examples.tsql:
WITH m AS (
  SELECT month_start, revenue,
         revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month_start) AS change_vs_prev
  FROM monthly_revenue
)
SELECT month_start, revenue, change_vs_prev
FROM m
WHERE month_start <= '2023-06-01'
ORDER BY month_start;

examples.title: Days since the customer's previous completed order
examples.explain_md: PARTITION BY customer restarts per customer; the first order of each customer is NULL. Customer 2's two orders on 2024-02-03 give 0 days. Cancelled and refunded orders are filtered out first, so they are not neighbours.
examples.mysql:
SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date,
       DATEDIFF(order_date, LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id)) AS days_since_prev
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed' AND customer_id IN (1, 2)
ORDER BY customer_id, order_date, order_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date,
       DATEDIFF(DAY, LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id), order_date) AS days_since_prev
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed' AND customer_id IN (1, 2)
ORDER BY customer_id, order_date, order_id;
examples.dialect_note_md: Argument order flips: MySQL `DATEDIFF(later, earlier)` has no unit; SQL Server `DATEDIFF(DAY, earlier, later)`. Writing the SQL Server order in MySQL would return a negative number.

examples.title: Minutes since the user's previous event
examples.explain_md: User 1 shows the 45-minute gap (09:10 to 09:55), the usual start of a new session. User 2's duplicate-timestamp events give 0. Each user's first event is NULL.
examples.mysql:
SELECT user_id, event_id, event_ts,
       TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE, LAG(event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_id), event_ts) AS minutes_since_prev
FROM events
ORDER BY user_id, event_ts, event_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT user_id, event_id, event_ts,
       DATEDIFF(MINUTE, LAG(event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_id), event_ts) AS minutes_since_prev
FROM events
ORDER BY user_id, event_ts, event_id;
examples.dialect_note_md: SQL Server `DATEDIFF(MINUTE, a, b)` counts minute-boundary crossings, not elapsed whole minutes: 09:59:59 to 10:00:01 is 1. MySQL `TIMESTAMPDIFF` truncates elapsed time. Identical on this data (all timestamps on whole minutes).

pitfalls_md: Swapping the argument order of `DATEDIFF` between dialects flips the sign or errors.
A time difference on the first row of a partition is NULL, not 0; wrap in `COALESCE` only if a default is truly meaningful.

sections.heading: FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE (and the frame trap)
sections.body_md:
- `FIRST_VALUE(expr)` returns `expr` from the first row of the window frame; `LAST_VALUE(expr)` from the last row.
- Default frame once there is an `ORDER BY`: `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`. The frame **ends at the current row**, so `LAST_VALUE` just returns the current row's own value (or a tied peer's).
- Fix 1: `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING` so the frame covers the whole partition.
- Fix 2 (no frame needed): `FIRST_VALUE` with the `ORDER BY` reversed. Last = first of the opposite order.
- `FIRST_VALUE` is safe with the default frame because the frame always starts at the partition start.
- `IGNORE NULLS` (skip NULLs when picking the value) is not available in MySQL, nor in SQL Server before 2022.

syntax.mysql:
FIRST_VALUE(expr) OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY o [frame])
LAST_VALUE(expr)  OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY o ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)
syntax.tsql:
FIRST_VALUE(expr) OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY o [frame])
LAST_VALUE(expr)  OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY o ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)

args.name: expr
args.meaning: Column or expression to return from the first/last frame row.

args.name: PARTITION BY p
args.meaning: Optional. First/last is taken per group.

args.name: ORDER BY o
args.meaning: Decides which row is 'first' and which is 'last'.

args.name: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
args.meaning: The frame that spans the whole partition. Mandatory for LAST_VALUE to see the true last row.

examples.title: FIRST_VALUE, broken LAST_VALUE, fixed LAST_VALUE
examples.explain_md: Per department, ordered by hire date. `last_default` simply echoes each row's own name (the frame ends at the current row). `last_fixed` uses the full frame and returns the newest hire for every row.
examples.mysql:
SELECT dept, name, hire_date,
       FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY hire_date) AS first_hired,
       LAST_VALUE(name)  OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY hire_date) AS last_default,
       LAST_VALUE(name)  OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY hire_date
                               ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_fixed
FROM employees
ORDER BY dept, hire_date;
examples.tsql:
SELECT dept, name, hire_date,
       FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY hire_date) AS first_hired,
       LAST_VALUE(name)  OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY hire_date) AS last_default,
       LAST_VALUE(name)  OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY hire_date
                               ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_fixed
FROM employees
ORDER BY dept, hire_date;

examples.title: Gap to the department's top salary
examples.explain_md: `FIRST_VALUE(salary)` over a descending order is the department maximum; subtract to get the gap. Jon's NULL salary yields a NULL gap, and Marketing's top is Ivy because NULL sorts last under DESC.
examples.mysql:
SELECT dept, name, salary,
       FIRST_VALUE(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dept_top,
       FIRST_VALUE(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) - salary AS gap_to_top
FROM employees
ORDER BY dept, salary DESC, emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT dept, name, salary,
       FIRST_VALUE(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dept_top,
       FIRST_VALUE(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) - salary AS gap_to_top
FROM employees
ORDER BY dept, salary DESC, emp_id;

examples.title: Latest event per user without LAST_VALUE
examples.explain_md: Reverse the sort and take FIRST_VALUE: no frame clause needed. DISTINCT collapses the one row per event down to one row per user.
examples.mysql:
SELECT DISTINCT user_id,
       FIRST_VALUE(event_type) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC, event_id DESC) AS latest_event
FROM events
ORDER BY user_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT DISTINCT user_id,
       FIRST_VALUE(event_type) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC, event_id DESC) AS latest_event
FROM events
ORDER BY user_id;

pitfalls_md: `LAST_VALUE` with only `ORDER BY` is the single most common window-function bug: it silently returns the current row.
With default `RANGE` framing, rows tied on the ORDER BY key are peers and all count as 'current'; `ROWS` treats them one at a time.
These functions return one row per input row. Use `DISTINCT` or `ROW_NUMBER() = 1` to get one row per group.

sections.heading: NTH_VALUE
sections.body_md:
- `NTH_VALUE(expr, n)` returns `expr` from the n-th row of the frame (1-based). NULL if the frame has fewer than n rows.
- Same frame trap as `LAST_VALUE`: the default frame stops at the current row, so early rows see NULL for n beyond their position. Use the full `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING` frame to read the n-th row of the whole partition.
- **SQL Server has no `NTH_VALUE`.** Emulate with `ROW_NUMBER()` and `MAX(CASE WHEN rn = n THEN expr END)`, which works in MySQL too.
- MySQL's `NTH_VALUE` also has `FROM FIRST/LAST` and `RESPECT/IGNORE NULLS` syntax, but only `FROM FIRST` and `RESPECT NULLS` are implemented.

syntax.mysql: NTH_VALUE(expr, n) OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY o ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)
syntax.tsql:
-- not available; emulate:
MAX(CASE WHEN rn = n THEN expr END)  -- rn from ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY o)

args.name: n
args.meaning: Which row of the frame, counting from 1. Must be a positive integer constant.

args.name: frame
args.meaning: Without the full frame, rows before the n-th see NULL.

examples.title: 2nd hire per department, default frame vs full frame
examples.explain_md: `second_default` is NULL until the window has seen two rows, so each department's first row shows NULL. `second_full` gives the true second hire on every row. Departments with one person (Exec) are always NULL.
examples.mysql:
SELECT dept, name, hire_date,
       NTH_VALUE(name, 2) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY hire_date) AS second_default,
       NTH_VALUE(name, 2) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY hire_date
                                ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS second_full
FROM employees
ORDER BY dept, hire_date;
examples.dialect_note_md: SQL Server has no `NTH_VALUE`. See the next example for the portable emulation.

examples.title: 2nd hire per department, portable emulation
examples.explain_md: `ROW_NUMBER` numbers the hires; `MAX(CASE WHEN rn = 2 ...)` picks the second per department. Departments without a second hire get NULL. Works unchanged in SQL Server.
examples.mysql:
SELECT dept,
       MAX(CASE WHEN rn = 2 THEN name END) AS second_hired
FROM (
  SELECT dept, name,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY hire_date) AS rn
  FROM employees
) t
GROUP BY dept
ORDER BY dept;
examples.tsql:
SELECT dept,
       MAX(CASE WHEN rn = 2 THEN name END) AS second_hired
FROM (
  SELECT dept, name,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY hire_date) AS rn
  FROM employees
) t
GROUP BY dept
ORDER BY dept;

pitfalls_md: If the frame has fewer than `n` rows, NTH_VALUE returns NULL, not an error.

sections.heading: Detecting changes: value <> LAG(value)
sections.body_md:
- Compare each row to the previous one in the same group: `value <> LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY t)`.
- On the first row `LAG` is NULL, so `<>` is UNKNOWN. Treat that row explicitly: `prev IS NULL OR value <> prev` (the first row is a change from 'nothing').
- NULL-safe alternative in MySQL only: `NOT (value <=> prev)`. SQL Server has no `<=>`; stay with the explicit `IS NULL` test.
- A 0/1 change flag, then a running `SUM` of the flag, labels each run of identical values with an island number. This is the start of gaps-and-islands.
- Window functions cannot be used in `WHERE`: compute the flag in a CTE, filter outside.

syntax.mysql:
CASE WHEN prev IS NULL OR value <> prev THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS changed
-- prev = LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY t)
syntax.tsql: CASE WHEN prev IS NULL OR value <> prev THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS changed

args.name: prev
args.meaning: LAG(value) in the same PARTITION BY / ORDER BY.

args.name: prev IS NULL
args.meaning: True only on the first row of each partition (or when the previous value really is NULL).

args.name: value <> prev
args.meaning: True when the value differs from the previous row.

args.name: THEN 1 ELSE 0
args.meaning: A numeric flag, so it can be summed for run numbers.

examples.title: Flag each change of event type per user
examples.explain_md: User 1 changes type on every event. User 2's second `view` repeats the first, so its flag is 0; user 3's second `view` also repeats.
examples.mysql:
WITH x AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_id, event_ts, event_type,
         LAG(event_type) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_id) AS prev_type
  FROM events
)
SELECT user_id, event_id, event_type, prev_type,
       CASE WHEN prev_type IS NULL OR event_type <> prev_type THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS changed
FROM x
ORDER BY user_id, event_ts, event_id;
examples.tsql:
WITH x AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_id, event_ts, event_type,
         LAG(event_type) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_id) AS prev_type
  FROM events
)
SELECT user_id, event_id, event_type, prev_type,
       CASE WHEN prev_type IS NULL OR event_type <> prev_type THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS changed
FROM x
ORDER BY user_id, event_ts, event_id;

examples.title: Keep only the rows where the type changed
examples.explain_md: Filter on the flag in an outer query. Repeated events are dropped, leaving the sequence of distinct steps.
examples.mysql:
WITH x AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_id, event_ts, event_type,
         LAG(event_type) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_id) AS prev_type
  FROM events
)
SELECT user_id, event_id, event_type
FROM x
WHERE prev_type IS NULL OR event_type <> prev_type
ORDER BY user_id, event_ts, event_id;
examples.tsql:
WITH x AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_id, event_ts, event_type,
         LAG(event_type) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_id) AS prev_type
  FROM events
)
SELECT user_id, event_id, event_type
FROM x
WHERE prev_type IS NULL OR event_type <> prev_type
ORDER BY user_id, event_ts, event_id;

examples.title: Number the runs of consecutive identical events
examples.explain_md: Running `SUM` of the change flag gives a run id that only increases at a change. User 2's two `view` events share run 1; user 3's later `view` after a purchase is run 3.
examples.mysql:
WITH x AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_id, event_ts, event_type,
         CASE WHEN LAG(event_type) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_id) IS NULL
                OR LAG(event_type) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_id) <> event_type
              THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS changed
  FROM events
)
SELECT user_id, event_id, event_type,
       SUM(changed) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_id
                          ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS run_id
FROM x
ORDER BY user_id, event_ts, event_id;
examples.tsql:
WITH x AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_id, event_ts, event_type,
         CASE WHEN LAG(event_type) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_id) IS NULL
                OR LAG(event_type) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_id) <> event_type
              THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS changed
  FROM events
)
SELECT user_id, event_id, event_type,
       SUM(changed) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_id
                          ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS run_id
FROM x
ORDER BY user_id, event_ts, event_id;

pitfalls_md: Writing `WHERE value <> LAG(value) OVER (...)` is invalid: windows cannot appear in `WHERE`.
Forgetting the `prev IS NULL` branch drops the first row of every group from the 'changes' result.
The same-second events of user 2 need an extra sort key (`event_id`); otherwise the order of the two `view` rows is undefined.
